A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neural amortized Bayesian actor framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: Sections 5.2–5.4 and Appendix D report original parameter-recovery simulations, identifiability analyses and Bayesian fits to previously collected human bean-bag data.

after.justification: Sections 4.2–4.5 and Appendix F report original simulations, a controlled identifiability experiment and cost-model comparisons using three human sensorimotor datasets.

M1.justification: v2 adds concrete actor-model losses: absolute, inverted Gaussian, absolute cost with quadratic effort, and Linex, with applicable cost parameters inferred (Appendix E). These extend the modeled cost options within the existing framework; the neural architecture, general training objective, reparameterization and NUTS inference procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Human-data coverage expands from bean-bag throwing to include virtual puck sliding and force reproduction (Section 4.5), introducing different response requirements and feedback environments. Section 4.4 additionally evaluates simulated behavior across two perceptual-uncertainty conditions.

E2.justification: v1's human-data example fits only quadratic cost with quadratic effort. v2 compares seven cost models, adding absolute, quadratic, inverted Gaussian, absolute cost with quadratic effort, asymmetric quadratic and Linex alternatives within that experiment (Figure 5, Table E.1). Synthetic comparisons against analytical solutions remain.

E3.justification: v2 introduces PSIS-LOO expected log predictive density for human-model comparison. Its new identifiability experiment uses 45 trials at each of two perceptual-uncertainty levels, 0.1 and 0.2, against 90-trial single-level controls. The retained 60-trial recovery experiments and neural-network training settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's tests fixing a confounded parameter, v2 tests whether varying perceptual uncertainty permits simultaneous estimation of prior and cost, with controls matching total trial count (Section 4.4, Figure 4). Figure 5 also examines sensitivity of inferred prior means to cost choice. Earlier confounding analyses are retained, partly in Appendix F.2.

E5.justification: Figure 5C newly reports standard errors for predictive-score differences. v2 also explicitly documents four chains and R-hat below 1.05 for human fits. Existing 94% posterior intervals and synthetic sampling counts remain; the PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: New Figure 4 reports tighter, less correlated prior–effort posteriors under two uncertainty levels. Figure 5 adds model rankings: a slight asymmetric-quadratic advantage for bean-bag data, inconclusive puck comparisons, and absolute cost with quadratic effort best and Linex worst for force reproduction. The earlier two-subject illustration is replaced. Recovery tables D.1–D.3 and F.1–F.3 retain identical numerical values.

T1.justification: Table E.1 adds explicit mathematical definitions for four newly evaluated cost families. The Bayesian decision equations, log-normal posterior and optimal-action derivations for quadratic and quadratic-effort costs are retained (v1 Appendix B; v2 Appendix C). The new disentangling evidence is a simulation, not a new proof.

C1.justification: v2's abstract and introduction add principled model comparison as an explicit contribution and strengthen the identifiability contribution from exposing confounding to demonstrating how experimental design can disentangle priors and costs. Empirical claims expand from bean-bag behavior to three sensorimotor tasks, while the central amortization and recovery claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 explains why perceptual uncertainty changes the influence of priors differently from costs and gives more specific experimental-design guidance. It also interprets the puck data as insufficient to distinguish cost models and the force example as showing model-dependent prior inference. The principal limitation requiring sampling from the observer's posterior remains.

D1.justification: v2 reports a public code repository and setup/run instructions, replacing v1's promised future release, and adds a reproducibility statement. The laptop and Intel CPU specification is removed. Existing optimizer settings, training budget, prior specifications and reported runtimes are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the puck and force dataset sources, connects the identifiability remedy to Wei and Hahn (2024), and discusses optimality criticism using Rahnev and Denison (2018). The Fechner citation is removed. Positioning relative to Acerbi et al. and Neupärtl and Rothkopf remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Much of the original exposition remains, with localized rewriting and shortening, unnumbered Related Work, and relocation of the quadratic-effort analysis to Appendix F.2. Broader impacts becomes an Ethics Statement, and a Reproducibility Statement is added. Author affiliations, publication headers and citation style also change.

P2.justification: Figure 5 is substantially redesigned from two-subject predictions, posterior densities and cost heatmaps into a three-task comparison with cost curves, prior intervals and predictive-score bars. v2 adds Figure 4 and Table E.1, splits the old Figure 4 between Figure 3 and Figure F.2, and moves the old Figure 2 to Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v2 tests an experimental-design remedy that v1 only recommended, using equal-trial controls, and replaces a single-task fit demonstration with uncertainty-aware comparisons of seven costs across three tasks. This substantially strengthens practical validation and guidance while retaining the original analytical recovery checks. Code access is better documented. The remedy remains demonstrated in a specific simulated setting and human examples remain illustrative, but these limits do not outweigh the gains.
